summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official Russian government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Kabardino-Balkaria, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The same note documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people running from 2017 to 2024 and records that the 2023 "extremist" designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; working in exile, he attests to annual deterioration across the region.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in Russia. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The regional pattern is not contained by borders: the UK Home Office note records violence spreading beyond the North Caucasus, and Isteev's account of annual deterioration describes a trajectory shared across the wider region rather than a condition unique to one republic.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kabardino-Balkaria cannot change the gender marker on Russian identity documents or access gender-affirming care, both prohibited by the 2023 federal law on gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes.

LGBT+ organising is exposed under the extremist designation to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, and 6 to 10 years where the activity is treated as organising; displaying alleged symbols of the designated movement has produced convictions under both the administrative and criminal codes. Public expression that justifies gender transition is separately criminalised by the expanded propaganda statute and attracts administrative fines.

Regional residents have been the target of systematic campaigns since 2017, continuing through 2024, and Isteev reports that family pressure can return a person to relatives who initiated the harm, with detention as a consequence of even private, undisclosed existence.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims, and treats the North Caucasus as a region where persecution is likely for trans people and public advocates.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no case-level record of violence against transgender people specifically within Kabardino-Balkaria; the documented trans-specific incident (the Novosibirsk conversion-therapy case) occurred elsewhere in Russia and is cited as evidence of the national pattern of coercion.

Whether Kabardino-Balkarian authorities initiate extremism prosecutions at a rate above or below the Russian national average is not sourced here; the figures cited (101 convictions as of 30 June 2025, eighteenfold growth in propaganda cases) are countrywide.

Entry and visa screening practice for transgender travellers arriving at Kabardino-Balkarian points of entry, and any republic-level variations in document checks, remain unresolved in this inventory.

Access to HIV care, mental-health services and legal aid for trans residents within the republic is not covered by the sources reviewed and is unresolved rather than assessed as absent.
